verdicts.trueWording: all of that is condensed into an epilogue
verdicts.note: Raw source reached: the talk's own transcript (introduction-guy-gavriel-kaydefault.srt, linked from the writersinspire page as 'A transcript/subtitles file (.srt) is available here'). In the Under Heaven passage Olley says almost the entirety of the rebellion itself, the years of upheaval it begins, the victories, the losses, the alliances, the political manoeuvrings, all condensed into an epilogue. Every limb supported. Only naming caveat: the auto-generated transcript renders 'An Shi/An Lushan' phonetically as 'the and Xi rebellion' earlier in the talk, so the rebellion's proper name is identified by context, not spelled on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: to look back with the tragic clarity of hindsight
verdicts.note: Same transcript, paragraph immediately after the Under Heaven discussion: rather than building up suspense, Kay chooses instead to encourage reflection, to look back with the tragic clarity of hindsight rather than to look forward with bated breath. Quote word for word; both limbs (suspense vs reflection; hindsight vs bated breath) present.

verdicts.trueWording: little interest in hitting the predictable beats of the historical period
verdicts.note: Same transcript, in the section on Kay crediting readers with historical knowledge, just before the Under Heaven example. The following sentence supplies the second limb: choosing instead to focus on the smaller, more personal moments behind the scenes which shape and motivate those larger events. Claim's 'a historical period' vs page's 'the historical period' is the only wording difference.

verdicts.trueWording: By allowing for a change in register
verdicts.note: Raw source reached: verse-and-prose-fantasy-literaturedefault.srt, the transcript linked from the writersinspire page. In the passage on embedding poetry at critical points, Olley says it works by allowing for a change in register, usually (as she concedes) into a more melancholic or portentous key, then illustrates with the lament for Boromir. Both limbs supported; the lecture's whole frame is prosimetrum, the alternation of verse and prose.

verdicts.trueWording: River of Stars is never showy
verdicts.note: Second body paragraph ('The plot is unremarkable when viewed from afar...'). Full sentence supplies both limbs: despite its ambition and length, and the clearly painstaking research behind it, River of Stars is never showy.

verdicts.trueWording: Kay's lyrical prose retains a sense of contemplative calm
verdicts.note: Located exactly where the claim says, in the paragraph beginning 'Not only are Shan and Daiyan wonderfully drawn characters'; the sentence continues 'even in the midst of brutal, heated battles, sieges, and ambushes', supporting the battles-and-ambushes limb.

verdicts.trueWording: appear for a mere scene before fading back into the narrative
verdicts.note: First body paragraph, closing sentence: Das explains Kay tells the story through an incredibly large cast of characters, some of whom do this. Both limbs (large cast; single scene then receding) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: the small moments that linger between the momentous ones
verdicts.note: Paragraph beginning 'Any historical period, any story of any major figure', as the claim states: Kay makes sure River of Stars always comes back to the individual people, the details, these small moments, likened to fine calligraphy under a looking glass.

verdicts.trueWording: Small events can be important in the unfolding
verdicts.note: The block quotation Das sets off and cites as p. 315 opens with this sentence, which continues 'like a pleated sail, of a world' and then instances an emissary's survival or drowning. The claim's characterisation of the passage's opening is exact.

verdicts.trueWording: the last book will bleed into the next one, the diction
verdicts.note: BrightWeavings reproduction of the Halasz NYRSF interview (page states it appears courtesy of Peter Halasz, who interviewed GGK for the New York Review of Science Fiction during 2000). Answer to 'Does one form of writing inform the other?', on script writing as a bridge out of one book into the next: Kay says he is always worried, and the sentence ends '...the style, the rhythms', supporting all three of diction, style and rhythms.

verdicts.trueWording: the writing changes in every book
verdicts.note: Verbatim, closing his answer 'But what dies when a nation is built?' about the last poem in the Lions epilogue: 'Anyway, the point is that that the writing changes in every book.' The claim's section hint ('answer on style and tone changing between books') points one answer earlier ('I think each book is different. The style and tone changes.'); the quoted sentence sits in the next answer of the same exchange. Claim itself fully supported.

verdicts.trueWording: strong "tile" of a charioteer, a strong "tile" of a senator
verdicts.note: Answer to the one-word question 'Rhythms?': Kay says the prologue of Sailing to Sarantium was written as a mosaic, built of these two tiles and 'strong contrasting tiles', and explains that in mosaic you contrast colours rather than blend them. Every limb (Sailing to Sarantium, prologue, contrasting tiles, charioteer, senator) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: influenced by the metaphor and the protagonist as a mosaicist
verdicts.note: Same answer on the prologue as mosaic, two sentences after the tiles: 'The style of this book, is influenced by the metaphor and the protagonist as a mosaicist.' 'This book' is Sailing to Sarantium, the book named at the start of that answer.

verdicts.trueWording: brief lives of the two troubadours at the beginning and end
verdicts.note: Answer on style and tone changing between books, as the claim's section hint says: Arbonne was written as a love song, the title gives it away, and the formal brief lives of the two troubadours at the beginning and end are meant to signal that the whole book is a song. 'Frame' is supported by 'at the beginning and end'.

verdicts.trueWording: What details do I need? Details are critical.
verdicts.note: Answer on layering up a scene: Kay describes his painterly method of layering, looking at the written scene the next morning and asking himself 'How do I flesh this out?', 'What details do I need?', then 'Details are critical.' Both limbs supported; the drafted-scene limb is explicit in 'I'll look at the written scene and ask myself'.
